doc.title: Eric Alexander interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: How he judges his playing and staying even-keeled
summary: He is more comfortable with his playing than ever but never satisfied, and values consistency over great nights.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: I can’t imagine that, because you seem to have the passion and the drive to keep going, which sort of begs the questions, at what level do you ever say, okay, this is where I wanted to be? Are you there now or do you just like not have a specific level in mind?

Well I think it’s less specific than that. It’s almost — well first of all I can say that I’m more comfortable with my playing than I’ve ever been. You know, I feel better about it. That’s the first part of it. But second, I’m not satisfied either. And it really comes down to, you know, gig to gig. You know sometimes I’ll go out on a gig and I’ll feel great and feel like I can do anything that I wanted to do. And I’ll have to say well it’s never so good it couldn’t get better, and then the next gig you go out and you don’t feel good, you feel like you played really poorly and you say well it’s not so bad, it couldn’t be worse. You have to have a real even keel about how you react to how you’re doing because some days are great but there are going to be just as many days that aren’t so great. And you can’t beat yourself up, but you also can’t get cocky if you’re doing well. You know you just have to stay focused and it’s kind of philosophical. You have an ideal in your mind of what would be perfect and you just keep moving towards it, but that ideal morphs and changes over the years too so you’ll never get there. It’s like chasing a rainbow.

I sometimes wonder if you watch basketball players for instance, and they have this tremendous night, everything’s falling and they’re in the right place at the right time and I wonder if they think why can’t I do that every night?

I’m sure they do. But I think, you know, (a) through experience they know that they can’t, and (b) they realize that often times the truth is you want your worst to be good enough, or your average to be better than most. If you’re great, okay it’s going to be great. And anybody — every dog has his day — everyone can have a great day. But you want to get to the point where your average performance is pretty damn good I guess. Consistency is important.
